records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's page title parenthetical leads with Carolina Jessamine (its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, in the same order), and its Description opens with 'Carolina jessamine'; RHS's page title pairs the binomial with evening trumpet flower, and its Other common names line reads Carolina jasmine, Carolina yellow jasmine, false jasmine, yellow jessamine. Carolina Jessamine, NC State's lead, is used. NC State's structured often-confused-with module lists Gelsemium rankinii, a separate species.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Gelsemium sempervirens page): a page-top banner reads 'This plant has high severity poison characteristics.' and points to its Poisonous to Humans block, which is human-scoped: Poison Severity: High. Poison Symptoms: Sweating, nausea, muscular weakness, dilated pupils, lowered temperature, convulsions, respiratory failure. Poison Toxic Principle: Alkaloids. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No, while the page's tag list also carries #contact dermatitis. Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Problems: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Children, Weedy. Plant Type: Ground Cover, Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Vine. The NC State page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. RHS (Potentially harmful): 'Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'; its only pet line is scoped to poultry: 'Pets (poultry): Harmful if eaten.' NC State's Poison Part list names every part from bark to seeds; RHS says harmful if eaten without naming a part. No admissible source names cats or dogs (RHS's pet line names poultry only), so toxic_to_pets is left null.
unknowns: Honeybee warning, beside attracts_pollinators true: NC State's plant-problems note reads 'Toxic pollen from this plant is detrimental to honeybee colonies. This plant is not suitable for beekeepers.' attracts_pollinators is true on NC State's Attracts field (Bees, Butterflies, Hummingbirds, Pollinators, Small Mammals): the plant draws bees, but its pollen harms honeybee colonies.

toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source names cats or dogs. NC State's Poison block is human-scoped (Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Children) with no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs value, and RHS's only pet line is 'Pets (poultry): Harmful if eaten.' Clemson's and MoBot's toxicity sentences (read in a browser by the researcher; see below) name no animal. No ASPCA entry used.

Toxicity scope: NC State's Poison Part list names every part (Bark through Stems), and its Causes Contact Dermatitis field says No while its tag list carries #contact dermatitis. Two pages read in a browser by the researcher, and confirmed by the auditor, are not cited because the quote checker cannot fetch them. Clemson HGIC's factsheet (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/carolina-jessamine/, HTTP 403 here) says under Problems 'All parts of this plant are very poisonous. The sap may cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals. Children can be poisoned by sucking the nectar from the flowers.' Missouri Botanical Garden's page (taxonid 282490) scopes it more narrowly: 'Flowers and foliage are poisonous if ingested.'

is_edible is false on RHS's Potentially harmful field ('Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling') and NC State's human-scoped Poison block, whose Poison Part list runs from bark to seeds; no admissible source describes any food use. The research record rested is_edible on MoBot's 'Flowers and foliage are poisonous if ingested.', which agrees but is not cited (MoBot refuses this machine).

RHS has a dedicated Gelsemium sempervirens page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/33397/gelsemium-sempervirens/details), Name Status Correct, page title Gelsemium sempervirens | evening trumpet flower, Other common names Carolina jasmine, Carolina yellow jasmine, false jasmine, yellow jessamine. Its structured fields read Position Full sun, Partial shade; Moisture Moist but well–drained; pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral; Hardiness H3 (a UK survival rating, not a damage onset); Max Height 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in) and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in), far narrower than NC State's 20-30 ft width. Its Potentially harmful field reads Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling, and its only pet line is Pets (poultry): Harmful if eaten. (poultry, not cats or dogs). It carries no pollinator tag, and its Cultivation paragraph is UK under-glass culture (Grow under glass in a peat-free, loam-based potting compost...), which supplies no field. UF/IFAS EDIS results were multi-species lists only, not a dedicated page, so not used.

Size: climbs is true, so mature_height_in 120-240 lands as the climber's reach, from NC State's Dimensions block (Height: 10 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in.); NC State's Description frames it the same way: 'It may grow from 12 to 20 feet as a twining vine trained to an arbor or trellis after three to four growing seasons. If unsupported, it creates a bushy ground cover.' Other heights: RHS Max Height 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in); MoBot 12-20 ft; and Clemson, by the researcher's paraphrase, 20 feet or more as a vine or 3 feet or less as a pruned ground cover. The MoBot and Clemson figures were read in a browser by the researcher and are not cited. The spread pair is null; see the mature_spread_in entry.

water_regime left null: NC State's 'Carolina jessamine is best grown in moist, organically rich, well-drained soils in full sun.' and RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' describe soil, not a watering instruction; NC State also calls the plant 'moderately tolerant of salt, wet soil or short periods of drought', and its Occasional Flooding value is a tolerance only. Clemson's 'Moist soil is ideal' and MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' (a mid-scale value that would not support keep_moist) were read in a browser by the researcher and are not cited.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), all open-ended or spanning, and RHS's pH field reads Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so neither a floor nor a ceiling can be set.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade and RHS's structured Position field reads Full sun, Partial shade, so part_shade rests on two structured fields. NC State says flowering is best in sun (Although it will tolerate light shade, best flowering and growth occur in sun.). Two pages read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor, and not cited because the quote checker cannot fetch them, agree on the sun preference: MoBot's structured Sun field is Full sun only (Tolerates light shade, but best flowering and growth occur in full sun.), and Clemson says it tolerates either full sun or partial shade (Flowering is more prolific and foliage growth is denser in full sun.). direct_sun_hours_max left null (NC State hour ranges come from a site-wide legend).

Fertilizer fields left null: no checked admissible page gives an interval, months or a dilution strength. Clemson's factsheet (read in a browser by the researcher; not cited) gives 'moderate amounts of a slow-release, balanced fertilizer, such as a 12-6-6', a formulation rather than a strength, and RHS's monthly liquid feed belongs to its UK under-glass culture.

Hardiness and chill: NC State's USDA zones 6a-10b and RHS's H3 are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures, so chill_damage_f is null (MoBot's zones 7-10, zone 6 if sheltered, and Clemson's zones 6-9 were read in a browser by the researcher; not cited). Temperatures, humidity and light fc are not addressed by admissible sources.
NC State fire note: 'This plant has a high flammability rating and should not be planted within the defensible space of your home.' (MoBot agrees, per the researcher's browser read; not cited.)

Clemson's factsheet (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/carolina-jessamine/) returns HTTP 403 to this machine and Missouri Botanical Garden's page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=282490) refuses it, so the quote checker cannot confirm either; the researcher read both in a browser. A value may rest on Clemson or MoBot only when the checker confirms its quote, so their ten research citations were dropped at landing, what they say is kept in these unknowns, and soil_base and is_edible were re-cited to NC State and RHS.

mature_spread_in_min and mature_spread_in_max are null at landing: the three dedicated pages disagree by an order of magnitude. NC State's Dimensions block reads 'Width: 20 ft. 0 in. - 30 ft. 0 in.' (240-360 in); RHS's Max Spread reads '0.5-1 metres' (19.7-39.4 in); Missouri Botanical Garden's Spread is 3-6 ft (36-72 in), by the researcher's browser read (not cited). NC State's 20-30 ft reads as the vine's sprawl (its Description adds 'If unsupported, it creates a bushy ground cover.'), and landing it would tell a vine grown on a fence that it spreads to 30 ft.
climbs is true: NC State's Quick ID Hints read 'Thin, wiry, evergreen vine that climbs by twining', its Climbing Method field reads Twining, and RHS's Habit field reads Climbing.

soil_base garden_bed rests on NC State's Landscape Location field (Naturalized Area, Vertical Spaces, Woodland; no container entry). The researcher's citation, Clemson's 'For best results, plant it in rich, well-drained soil.', cannot be checked from here and was dropped. NC State's Description also lists planters among the vertical spaces the vine suits ('trellises, arbors, fences, planters, porch columns, and screens'), and RHS's UK culture is under glass in potting compost.

is_houseplant false: no admissible page frames it as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field lists Ground Cover, Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous and Vine, and its USDA zones are 6a-10b. RHS's UK culture is under glass, with Patio and container plants among its suggested planting locations, which is greenhouse and patio culture, not houseplant culture.

Not a Jasminum: RHS's Family field reads Gelsemiaceae and NC State's Description calls it 'a member of the yellow-jessamine family (Gelsemiaceae)' (NC State's Family attribute reads Loganiaceae). Nothing was taken from the landed Jasminum officinale (Common Jasmine) or Trachelospermum jasminoides (Star Jasmine) records, or from the swamp jessamine Gelsemium rankinii. MoBot's alternate names 'Carolina yellow jasmine' (its Common Name line) and 'false jasmine or false jessamine' (its prose) were read in a browser by the researcher; not cited.

records.name_note: Sources split on the common name. NC State's page title parenthetical lists Japanese Clematis first (the list is alphabetized) and its description prose opens with 'Japanese clematis'; the same list also carries Sweet Autumn Clematis. Clemson HGIC's dedicated page is titled 'Invasive Plant Spotlight: Sweet Autumn Clematis', and the RHS browser page title reads 'Clematis terniflora | sweet autumn clematis'. Common_name follows NC State's lead. NC State also lists the previously-known-as names Clematis cuspidatum, Clematis dioscoreifolia and Clematis maximowicziana, and RHS's Synonyms list includes Clematis paniculata Thunb. NC State's 'is often confused with' module names Clematis recta and Clematis virginiana.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu, Clematis terniflora page): the page states 'This plant has high severity poison characteristics.' Under its 'Poisonous to Humans' heading, Poison Severity is High (a human-scoped rating; the Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags are separate). Poison Symptoms text: 'Clematis can cause severe mouth pain and ulcers if eaten. Toxic to dogs, cats, horses. Clinical signs are salivation, vomiting, diarrhea. In humans, symptoms may include dizziness, confusion, fainting, and convulsions. Fatalities are rare, due to the rapid and intense bitter taste and mouth irritation from eating. Gastric lavage is recommended and anti-inflammatory to soothe irritated tissue.' Poison Toxic Principle: protoanemonin. Poison Part: Leaves, Sap/Juice. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; the Poison Symptoms value closes with the handling warning 'Contact dermatitis results in skin redness and burning sensation for some people, gardening gloves are recommended.' The Problems field lists: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy. Whole Plant Traits, Plant Type (six values): Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Shrub, Vine, Weed. NC State also states it is listed as invasive by the NC Invasive Plant Council and 'not recommended for any garden' (recorded as stated, not as care). RHS scopes its harm warning differently: 'Skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' and 'Pets (rabbits): Harmful if eaten.' (rabbits only, no cat/dog scope). ASPCA is not an admissible source here. No admissible source states the plant is eaten as food.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated Clematis terniflora page (kempercode a300, served from plantfinder.mobot.org) renders in a browser but fails to the sandboxed fetcher on its TLS certificate chain, so no field rests on it alone, and it is not cited. Read in a browser at audit, it agrees with NC State on size (Height and Spread 15.00 to 30.00 feet), gives Sun: Full sun to part shade (its Culture text adds that the plant 'will thrive and bloom well in considerable shade') and Water: Medium, and gives Common Name: sweet autumn virginsbower.

RHS's Synonyms list for Clematis terniflora includes 'Clematis paniculata Thunb.' (listed as a synonym; RHS marks only Clematis chinensis and Clematis thunbergii as misapplied). Missouri Botanical Garden's page, read in a browser at audit (not cited), says the plant is 'sometimes sold as' C. paniculata, 'although technically C. paniculata is a separate species native to New Zealand.' Nothing was taken from the landed Jackman's Clematis (b23) or from Clematis virginiana.

is_houseplant false: no admissible page addresses indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field lists Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Shrub, Vine and Weed, its USDA zones are 5a-9a, and RHS's suggested planting locations are Cottage and informal garden, Wildlife gardens, Climber and wall shrubs, and Wall side borders.

toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's 'Toxic to dogs, cats, horses' text and its Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags. RHS scopes pets to rabbits only. NC State's Poison Severity High is human-scoped.
is_edible is false on NC State's statement that 'Clematis can cause severe mouth pain and ulcers if eaten' and its Poisonous to Humans listing; no source describes any food use.

Invasive status and 'not recommended for any garden' are recorded only as NC State states them (listed as invasive by the NC Invasive Plant Council; 'an aggressive weed'); Clemson HGIC calls it a non-native invasive species reported invasive in at least 10 states. They are not care fields.

water_regime left null: RHS's structured Moisture field says 'Moist but well-drained' (used for soil_drainage = moderate), but no admissible source gives a watering statement; NC State gives only Good Drainage with no moisture tag. water_dry_down_target and day-interval fields left null for an in-ground vine.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: RHS pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (alkaline acceptable); NC State gives no pH.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours of direct sun, mapped to part_shade); RHS lists Full sun only. direct_sun_hours_max left null because no species-specific hour limit is stated.

Size follows NC State's Dimensions block (Height and Width each 15 ft. 0 in. - 30 ft. 0 in. = 180-360 in), and its prose says the plant may rapidly reach 15 to 30 feet high and wide. climbs is true, so the height lands as the climber's reach. RHS gives a taller Max Height of 8-12 metres (315-472 in) but a smaller Max Spread of 4-8 metres (157-315 in); disagreement noted, RHS not used. Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited) also gives Height and Spread of 15.00 to 30.00 feet, and its prose says that with support the vine climbs to 20-25 ft and that without support it sprawls as a ground cover 6-12 in tall and 10 ft wide; that sprawl figure is not used.
RHS's Cultivation paragraph ('moisture-retentive, well-drained soil', roots shaded) is genus-level boilerplate and was not used.
Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer and chill-damage fields have no admissible species-specific support; NC State zones 5a-9a is a hardiness range, not a damage onset.

climbs is true: NC State says 'It climbs other vegetation, forming dense blankets that block sunlight to the plants underneath.', its Habit/Form field lists Climbing and its Climbing Method field reads Twining; RHS describes a 'climber 6m tall or more' and its Habit field reads Climbing.

soil_base garden_bed rests on RHS's suggested planting locations (Cottage and informal garden, Wildlife gardens, Climber and wall shrubs, Wall side borders; no container entry). The research citation, NC State's Soil Texture value 'Loam (Silt)' (the field also lists Clay), was replaced: a texture field cannot tell a garden bed from a container.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox page for Prunus x cistena prints no Poison block, so no poison part, symptom list, toxic principle, severity rating or handling warning is given for this hybrid. Its only toxicity-related statements are its Problem-for designations, which it renders twice. The Tags line carries fourteen tags: #deciduous #showy leaves #foundation planting #red leaves #specimen #white flowers #spring flowers #bird friendly #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #full sun tolerant #frequent disease problems #frequent insect problems. The structured Problems field renders six values: Frequent Disease Problems, Frequent Insect Problems, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Short-lived. Neither names a plant part, symptom or severity for the animals. RHS's dedicated page for this hybrid carries no toxicity statement, and its only edibility words, 'Some have edible fruit in autumn', belong to its genus description, so no checked admissible source disagrees on scope or edibility. Nothing was borrowed from Prunus cerasifera or any other parent species page.
unknowns: NC State's dedicated Prunus x cistena page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/prunus-x-cistena/) is the anchor for every value. Two more admissible dedicated pages for this hybrid were read at audit. RHS's 'Prunus × cistena' profile (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/47608/prunus-%C3%97-cistena/details) gives Name Status 'Correct' and the common name 'purple-leaf sand cherry'. Missouri Botanical Garden's page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=263994), read by the auditor with the server's missing intermediate certificate supplied, is not cited: the quote checker cannot fetch it; it reads 'Common Name: purple-leaf sand cherry'. Both corroborate full sun (MoBot 'Sun: Full sun'; RHS Position 'Full sun, Partial shade') and moderate drainage (RHS Moisture 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'; MoBot 'Best grown in moist, organically rich, well-drained soils in full sun.'). Neither carries a toxicity or edibility statement for this hybrid; RHS's only edibility words, 'Some have edible fruit in autumn', are in its genus description and support nothing here. Neither names pollinators: MoBot gives 'Attracts: Birds', and RHS shows no pollinator listing. MoBot's 'Water: Medium' is a mid-scale rating that maps to no water_regime token, and MoBot rates 'Maintenance: Low' where NC State lists High. No dedicated Clemson HGIC page for this hybrid was found.

name_note left null: NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Purple Leaf Sand Cherry, Purple-leaf Sand Cherry) and its order matches the page-title parenthetical, and its description opens 'Purple Leaf Sand Cherry is a deciduous shrub in the rose family that matures at around 8 feet tall and wide.' RHS (and Missouri Botanical Garden, read at audit, not cited) write the same name hyphenated, 'purple-leaf sand cherry', which is NC State's second-listed spelling, so the dedicated pages agree on the name and differ only in the hyphen.

is_houseplant false: no admissible page frames this hybrid as a houseplant or mentions indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field renders Shrub and Tree, and its description says 'Plant it in the shrub in the border, as a specimen, near an entryway or as a foundation plant.'; RHS's suggested planting locations are City and courtyard gardens, Cottage and informal garden, and Flower borders and beds. Missouri Botanical Garden (read at audit, not cited) lists 'Type: Deciduous shrub'.

toxic_to_pets is true only on NC State's Problem-for designations, which the page renders twice: as the tags #problem for dogs, #problem for horses and #problem for cats, and as values of its structured Problems field (Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses, beside Frequent Disease Problems, Frequent Insect Problems and Short-lived). The page prints no Poison block, no poison part, no symptoms and no severity. RHS's page for this hybrid carries no toxicity statement, and neither does Missouri Botanical Garden's (read at audit, not cited).

is_edible left null: the page says only that birds eat the fruits (Wildlife Value) and never addresses human eating of this hybrid; edible-fruit claims for Prunus cerasifera were deliberately not borrowed.

attracts_pollinators left null: NC State's 'bird friendly' tag and 'Birds eat the fruits' wildlife value concern birds eating fruit, not pollinators; the page names no bees, butterflies or other pollinators.

water_regime left null: the page gives only soil adjectives (Good Drainage, Moist; 'prefers moist rich loams') and no watering statement. soil_drainage is moderate because Good Drainage + Moist is a preference, not a moisture_retentive requirement.

outdoor_sun_exposure lists only full_sun, on NC State's structured Light field, which lists full sun alone ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'); NC State treats shade only as a tolerance ('It will tolerate some shade but the best flowering and leaf color occur in full sun.'). RHS's Position field reads 'Full sun, Partial shade', and its Cultivation line says 'Easy to grow in any moist but well-drained moderately fertile soil in sun or partial shade. Superb hedging shrub'; part_shade is left out because the North American structured field excludes it. Missouri Botanical Garden (read at audit, not cited) agrees with NC State: 'Sun: Full sun' and 'Tolerates part shade, but best flowering and leaf color generally occur in full sun.' direct_sun_hours_max left null: no source gives a species-specific hour limit, and the 6-or-more-hours figure is NC State's light-category minimum.

soil_ph left null: NC State's page has no Soil pH field, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', which sets no numeric floor or ceiling. Temperatures, chill damage, humidity, fertilizing and watering intervals left null: no admissible source states them. NC State's USDA zones 2a-8b and RHS's hardiness rating H6 are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures (Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Zone: 2 to 8', read at audit, not cited, is the same).

Mature size uses NC State's Dimensions block on the hybrid's own page (Height 7-10 ft, Width 5-8 ft, converted to inches); its description prose separately says it 'matures at around 8 feet tall and wide'. RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of '1-1.5 metres' each (about 39-59 in) with a Time to Maturity of '10–20 years'. Missouri Botanical Garden (read at audit, not cited) gives 'Height: 6.00 to 10.00 feet' and 'Spread: 5.00 to 8.00 feet', the same spread and top height with a lower minimum. Neither was used; NC State's Dimensions block is the anchor.

NC State's description states it is short-lived 'to about 10 years due to insects and diseases', carries the tags 'frequent disease problems' and 'frequent insect problems', and lists Maintenance: High; these are reported only as stated. Cultivars 'Big Cis' and 'Minnesota Red' are listed but their descriptions support no field here.
soil_base garden_bed reflects that the page treats it as an in-ground landscape shrub (border, specimen, foundation plant); the page states no potting or container recommendation.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's description opens with 'Japanese euonymus', and its alphabetized common-name list (the page-title parenthetical) has Japanese Euonymus as its fourth entry, after Box-Leaf Euonymus, Dwarf Japanese Euonymus and Evergreen Euonymus. RHS's page title pairs the binomial with 'evergreen spindle', and RHS lists 'Japanese spindle tree' under Other common names. Japanese Euonymus was chosen because it is the prose opener on NC State's dedicated page.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (heading 'Poisonous to Humans', Poison block): Poison Severity is Low (the page banner reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.'), a human-scoped rating. Poison Symptoms: 'Vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, chills, coma, and convulsions when consumed in large quantities.' Poison Toxic Principle: 'Unidentified, possibly a glycoside'. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part (full list): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Plant Type tags: Poisonous, Shrub. Page tags include #poisonous and #poisonous if ingested. NC State's separate Edibility line reads 'Toxic if eaten in large quantities.' NC State carries no cat or dog tag on this page. RHS (Potentially harmful, Humans/Pets): 'Harmful if eaten; wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' The two sources differ on scope: NC State ties the effects to large quantities, while RHS says harmful if eaten with no quantity limit and adds a handling warning (gloves and protective equipment) that NC State does not carry. RHS names 'Pets' without naming cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets is left null.

toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's Poison block is human-scoped (Low severity) with no cat or dog tag, and RHS says 'Humans/Pets' without naming cats or dogs, which is an unscoped mention. No ASPCA entry is admissible or was found.

is_edible is false based on NC State's Edibility line ('Toxic if eaten in large quantities.') and RHS's 'Harmful if eaten'. NC State's wording is conditional on large quantities while RHS's is not; no source describes any edible use.

is_houseplant false: the admissible pages treat it as an outdoor shrub and do not address indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field lists Poisonous and Shrub, its USDA zones are 6a-9b and its Landscape Location field lists Naturalized Area and Woodland. RHS lists Patio and container plants among its suggested planting locations (with Coastal, City and courtyard gardens, Cottage and informal garden, Flower borders and beds, and Hedging and screens), which is outdoor container use, not houseplant culture.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and RHS lists acid or alkaline or neutral, so both ends are open.

water_regime and the other watering fields left null: no watering instruction was found. NC State's Soil Drainage values (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry) and RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well–drained or Well–drained') describe soil, not a watering rule. soil_drainage is moderate on NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair and RHS's 'Moist but well–drained'. NC State's prose that it 'does not do well in wet conditions' rules out moisture_retentive, and its note that it 'will grow in most soils, including clay' asks for no sharp, sandy drainage, so fast is not supported either.
chill_damage_f left null: RHS H5 and NC State zones 6a-9b are hardiness ratings, not a damage-onset temperature. RHS's H5 is a UK rating.

outdoor_sun_exposure maps NC State's Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade tags to part_shade and its Full sun tag to full_sun; RHS's Position field lists Full sun and Partial shade. NC State's prose says it 'tolerates full sun and heavy shade' but does best in sun-dappled conditions with 'some afternoon shade in hot summer climates'. full_sun rests on the two structured fields, not on that tolerance clause, and heavy shade appears only as a tolerance, so full_shade is not included.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: no species-specific prose gives an hours figure. The hours in NC State's light tags are the site-wide legend.

Size anchors on NC State's Dimensions block (Height: 10 ft. 0 in. - 15 ft. 0 in.; Width: 5 ft. 0 in. - 8 ft. 0 in.), which its Description repeats as 10 to 15 feet tall and 5 to 8 feet wide (120-180 and 60-96 in). RHS's Max Height of 2.5-4 metres (98-157 in) is lower than NC State's, and its Max Spread of 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in) is about the same. NC State notes it can reach 26 feet in height if left alone. NC State's cultivar sizes were not used.
attracts_pollinators left null: no Attracts field or pollinator statement was found on the admissible pages.
The epithet is spelled 'japonicus' on both NC State and RHS, and RHS lists Euonymus pulchellus as a synonym; neither affects the accepted name.

Spanish Bluebell was chosen because NC State and RHS both lead with it. RHS's Synonyms field lists Scilla hispanica and Scilla campanulata (with Endymion campanulatus and Hyacinthoides campanulata) for this same plant. NC State's "is often confused with" module for this page lists Hyacinthus orientalis and Muscari armeniacum.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Poisonous to Humans block): Poison Severity: High. Poison Symptoms: "HIGHLY TOXIC, MAY BE FATAL IF EATEN! SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Pain in the mouth, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, cramping, diarrhea, and lowered heart rate. Skin irritation in susceptible individuals." Poison Toxic Principle: Cardiac glycosides. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (full list): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. NC State's Problems tags on the page: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Weedy. Its Plant Type tags: Bulb, Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial. The severity rating and the symptom list come from the Poisonous to Humans block, which is human-scoped, and NC State carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag for this plant. RHS's dedicated Hyacinthoides hispanica profile (Potentially harmful field) reads: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits): Harmful if eaten." That RHS line is the only admissible statement naming cats or dogs, and it is why toxic_to_pets is true. RHS's "Harmful if eaten" is milder wording than NC State's "HIGHLY TOXIC, MAY BE FATAL IF EATEN!". Clemson HGIC (dedicated Wood Hyacinth page) says skin irritation is the most common toxic effect, advises wearing gloves when planting the bulbs if you have sensitive skin, and says "Bulbs or plant parts should never be eaten as they are highly poisonous." Clemson files it under Liliaceae, while NC State gives Asparagaceae.
unknowns: Cats and dogs: RHS's dedicated Hyacinthoides hispanica profile is the only admissible source that names them. Its Potentially harmful field reads "Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits): Harmful if eaten.", which supports toxic_to_pets true. NC State's poison block is human-scoped and carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag, and Clemson's toxicity sentences name no animal (its line "They’re deer- and rabbit-resistant." is about browsing, not poisoning).

Naturalizing and weediness: NC State says this plant is clump-forming, naturalizes easily and can become weedy, and lists Weedy among its Problems. Clemson says to give them room to spread, 'as they will be naturalized by seeds and bulblets.' Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor; not cited) says it 'Naturalizes well by both bulb offsets and self-seeding in optimum growing conditions.'

Hybridization: Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor; not cited) says 'Plants of this species (Spanish bluebells) will hybridize with plants of Hyancinthoides non-scripta (English bluebells) if planted near each other, resulting in different forms appearing through self-seeding.' (MoBot's spelling). Nothing was taken from any H. non-scripta or H. × massartiana page.

RHS's dedicated profile for this exact taxon (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/8882/hyacinthoides-hispanica/details; page title "Hyacinthoides hispanica | Spanish bluebell", Name Status Correct) gives a pH field of "Acid or Alkaline or Neutral". Because RHS lists alkaline soils as acceptable, the 8.0 top of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band is not landed as soil_ph_max, and soil_ph_min stays null because NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended. RHS rates the plant H6 and gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres (about 4-20 inches) and Max Spread 0-0.1 metre (0-4 inches). Its spread is far narrower than NC State's 6-12 inch width, and NC State's Dimensions block stays the size anchor. RHS also notes that this plant is listed as an invasive non-native species in Northern Ireland.

water_regime is null: no source gives a watering statement. NC State's 'moist, well-drained soil' and RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well–drained or Well–drained') describe soil, not watering; NC State also lists Dry Soil under Resistance To Challenges and tags the plant #drought tolerant. Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor; not cited) gives a structured 'Water: Medium', which is mid-scale, and 'average, medium moisture, well-drained soil', which is soil description.

chill_damage_f is null: NC State says the plant is 'Hardy II, injured at temperatures below 14 degrees F (-10C) when planted', which is a hardiness rating rather than a damage-onset temperature. Hardiness zones are 3a-8b (NC State) and 3 to 8 (Clemson; Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor; not cited) agrees), and RHS rates it H6.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun and Partial Shade; RHS's Position field reads "Full shade, Full sun, Partial shade". full_shade is left out: only RHS lists it, and NC State's North American structured Light field excludes it; Missouri Botanical Garden's Sun field, read in a browser at audit and not cited, reads "Full sun to part shade" and excludes it too. NC State's "tolerates full sun to full shade" and MoBot's "Tolerates shady conditions." are tolerance asides. part_sun is not listed because no structured field carries it; its only support is NC State's prose preference for "part sun or partial shade". NC State's prose treats full sun as tolerated rather than preferred, MoBot says "Perhaps best in sun-dappled part shade.", and Clemson advises "In our hot Southern climate, wood hyacinths are best planted where they get morning sun and shade in the afternoon".
direct_sun_hours_max is null: no species-specific hour figure outside NC State's generic light-category legend.

Size: NC State (Height 0 ft. 6 in. - 1 ft. 6 in.; Width 0 ft. 6 in. - 1 ft. 0 in.) is the anchor. Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor; not cited) gives Height 0.75 to 1.50 feet (9-18 in) and Spread 0.75 to 1.00 feet (9-12 in), slightly different at the low end; RHS's sizes are in the RHS entry above.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field lists Bulb, Ground Cover and Herbaceous Perennial and its USDA zones are 3a-8b; Container is one of its four Landscape Locations (with Naturalized Area, Small Space and Woodland), and its Description names pots last among outdoor uses.

Edibility: is_edible is false because Clemson says bulbs or plant parts should never be eaten as they are highly poisonous, and NC State says it may be fatal if eaten. No source describes any edible use.
Humidity, indoor temperature, indoor light, fertilizer and watering intervals are null: no admissible source covers them for this outdoor bulb.

soil_base garden_bed: NC State's Description lists woodland edge, groundcover under deciduous trees, rock gardens, woodland gardens, borders and beds before pots, and Clemson calls wood hyacinths 'a perfect choice for woodland areas'. Container is one of NC State's four Landscape Locations and it carries a #container plant tag; that container use is noted, not encoded.

Missouri Botanical Garden's page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=q740) refuses this machine, so its nine research citations were dropped at landing: a value may rest on MoBot only when the quote checker confirms its quote. Read in a browser by the researcher and the auditor, it gives 'Common Name: Spanish bluebell', 'Hyacinthoides hispanica, commonly called Spanish bluebell or wood hyacinth, is a bulbous perennial that is native to Spain, Portugal and northwest Africa.', 'Species is synonymous with and formerly known as Scilla campanulata, Scilla hispanica and Endymion hispanicus.', 'Family: Asparagaceae', 'Sun: Full sun to part shade' and 'Easily grown in average, medium moisture, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.' Endymion hispanicus, a synonym the batch named, appears on no page the checker can read; RHS lists Endymion campanulatus instead.

records.name_note: NC State lists Musa japonica under "Previously known as". NC State's "is often confused with" module for Musa basjoo names Strelitzia reginae. Common-name sources split on the lead name: NC State's page-title parenthetical begins "Basjoo Banana Tree" (its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and also contains Japanese Banana), while the RHS page for Musa basjoo is titled with "Japanese banana". Japanese Banana was chosen because it is the name RHS leads with and the name NC State's own description prose uses.
unknowns: The Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page for Musa basjoo (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=d442) refuses scripted fetches from this machine with a certificate error, so the quote checker cannot load it, and it is not cited; no value rests on it. It reads in a browser and was read at audit. It renders 'Common Name: Japanese banana', 'Sun: Full sun', 'Water: Medium', 'Height: 6.00 to 14.00 feet' and 'Spread: 6.00 to 14.00 feet'. Its Culture paragraph says 'It is best grown in organically rich, medium moisture, well-drained soil in full sun.', 'Plants tolerate and often appreciate some part shade or light filtered sun in the heat of the day.' and 'Best growth occurs with consistently moist soils that do not dry out.'
The only other admissible Musa pages found are UF/IFAS Musa spp.: Banana (ST409) and a Florida banana-growing guide. Both are genus-level or multi-species pages, so they were not used.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. Neither NC State nor RHS names Musa basjoo as toxic or non-toxic to cats or dogs, and no toxicity claim is made. NC State's Edibility field reads 'The fruits are inedible.' and is carried in is_edible. NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) says the stem, flower, leaves and rhizome have been used medicinally, which is not an edibility or toxicity statement.
is_edible=false rests on NC State's statement that the fruits are inedible, which RHS echoes ('inedible green fruits'). Neither source addresses eating any other part of the plant.

soil_drainage=moderate comes from NC State's structured Soil Drainage field, which renders exactly 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist', and from its prose 'moist, well-drained, humus-rich, or loam soils'. Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited) agrees: 'It is best grown in organically rich, medium moisture, well-drained soil in full sun.' For containers it says 'Keep container soils consistently moist but not wet.' Neither North American page asks for wet soil, so moisture_retentive is not supported. RHS's Moisture field reads only 'Well–drained', which is ambiguous on its own. water_regime=keep_moist rests on NC State's 'It grows best in consistently moist soils and should not be allowed to dry out.' MoBot's 'Best growth occurs with consistently moist soils that do not dry out.' agrees but is not cited. MoBot's structured row reads 'Water: Medium', a mid-scale value that does not itself support keep_moist; it is disclosed here as a counterpoint.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State tags Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'. The acid and alkaline bands are open-ended, so no floor or ceiling can be set.

outdoor_sun_exposure keeps full_sun and part_shade on NC State's structured Light field ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)') and its Description ('The Japanese banana prefers full sun to partial shade and moist, well-drained, humus-rich, or loam soils.'). RHS's structured Position field renders only 'Full sun'. The audit flagged part_shade for removal on the strength of Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited), whose structured row reads 'Sun: Full sun' and which treats shade only as a conditional tolerance ('Plants tolerate and often appreciate some part shade or light filtered sun in the heat of the day.'). Landing decision: part_shade is kept, because the only North American structured field that would exclude it is MoBot's, which the quote checker cannot confirm, and RHS's UK Position field alone does not exclude a value NC State's structured field lists. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures on NC State's page are its site-wide light-category legend.

chill_damage_f is null. NC State says the rhizomes are cold hardy to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit if pruned and mulched, and gives USDA zones 5 to 10. Those are survival and hardiness ratings, not a damage-onset temperature. RHS rates the plant H2 (UK scale), also a hardiness rating.

is_houseplant lands false: the indoor guidance on these pages is winter protection for container plants, not houseplant culture (the b86 African Blue Lily landing read the same guidance the same way). NC State says 'The Japanese banana is best used as a tropical specimen or a container plant. It can be brought indoors for winter before the first frost and placed in a sunny room for overwintering.' It carries the tag '#interiorscape' and notes 'Potential insect pests for indoor plants are aphids, spider mites, mealybugs, and scale.' Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited) says 'For container plants, bring container indoors in fall before first frost and place in a large sunny room for overwintering as a houseplant' and 'Watch for aphids, spider mites, mealybugs and scale on houseplants.' Its Uses paragraph says of bananas in general 'Whether grown outdoors in the landscape or indoors as a houseplant, bananas need lots of space.' RHS's plant-type badges read 'Conservatory Greenhouse' and 'Herbaceous Perennial'.

soil_base is null. NC State's cultural text mixes in-ground and container use, and RHS's potting-compost advice sits in a genus-style banana-cultivation paragraph. Neither supports a single soil_base token for this species.

RHS also lists Musa acuminata 'Basjoo' and Musa japonica as synonyms of this name and rates Name Status Correct for Musa basjoo. The catalog's separate Musa acuminata (Banana) record was not reused here.
Fertilizer: NC State only says to 'fertilize the plant regularly during the growing season'. No interval, months or dilution strength is stated, so all fertilize fields are null.

attracts_pollinators is null. NC State's Play Value says 'Attractive Flowers' and names no pollinator. Temperature, humidity and light-intensity fields are null because no source states them. Watering interval and dry-down fields are null because the plant is an in-ground perennial and no source frames watering that way.

Red Spider Lily is also one of the seven names in NC State's alphabetized page-title parenthetical. Sources split on the lead name: Clemson HGIC's page for this species is titled Spider Lilies; the more specific Red Spider Lily is used. NC State lists the previous name Amaryllis radiata, and RHS lists the synonym Nerine japonica; neither is used here. Other names in NC State's list are not used as the primary name.
records.toxicity_detail: Near the top of NC State's page, before its Description, it states "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." NC State's Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped) reads: Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "Causes only low toxicity if bulb is eaten. Abdominal pain, salivation, shivering, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea."; Poison Toxic Principle: "Lycorine, an alkaloid"; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Roots (the only part listed, although the symptoms line names the bulb). NC State's Problems field lists only "Poisonous to Humans"; the page carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs value. NC State's Plant Type field has three values (Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous), and its tags include #poisonous. RHS's Potentially harmful field reads "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and continues "Pets: Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers"; that Pets line names no animal, so it is not treated as cat or dog evidence. RHS's glove warning has no counterpart in NC State's block, which answers Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. No admissible source names cats or dogs for this species.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder (kempercode c535, which redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org) fails certificate verification for scripted fetches from this machine, so the researcher used no MoBot evidence, and no MoBot citation is landed: a value may rest on MoBot only when the quote checker confirms its quote. The audit read the page in a browser on 2026-10-03: "Common Name: spider lily", "Sun: Full sun to part shade", "Water: Medium", "Height: 1.00 to 2.00 feet", "Spread: 1.00 to 1.50 feet"; its Noteworthy Characteristics opens "Lycoris radiata, commonly called red spider lily, is a late summer-blooming bulb of the amaryllis family."; its Culture text says "Best flowering is in part shade." (as NC State says, while Clemson says it will bloom best with at least 4 hours of full sun), and the page makes no toxicity statement and names no cats or dogs.

toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source names cats or dogs for Lycoris radiata. RHS's Pets line names no animal; NC State's poison block is human-scoped and the page has no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag.
toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison Part field says Roots while its symptom line says low toxicity if bulb is eaten; RHS says ornamental bulbs are not to be eaten. Both set is_edible false.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State treats it as a landscape bulb but lists Container among its Landscape Locations and cautions "These bulbs require an extensive root system to produce flowers; therefore, if container planting is being considered, be sure the pot size is adequate." RHS tags it Conservatory Greenhouse, and Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited) says "In colder climates bulbs should be grown in large containers that are overwintered indoors." None of this is houseplant culture.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State gives a hardiness-style statement with two figures (semi-hardy damaged below 28 F to hardy injured below 5 F), not a single damage-onset temperature; RHS gives only H3 and Clemson a zone range of 6 to 10.

water_regime and the day-interval fields left null: NC State says rich, moist well-drained soil, fairly dry in dormancy, and avoid overwatering to prevent root rot, but gives no watering regime; the structured Moist tag is not a watering statement. RHS's Cultivation text (fertile, well-drained soil that dries out in summer) was not used: it is RHS's shared Lycoris wording, word for word on its Lycoris aurea page (see the last entry).
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), whose outer bands are open-ended, and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral.

Sun: Clemson says sun to part shade and blooms best with at least 4 hours of full sun (a minimum, not a maximum), so direct_sun_hours_max is null. RHS lists Full sun only; NC State's structured Light field lists both Full sun and Partial Shade, so both are kept.

Size: NC State's species page (Height and Width both 1 ft. 0 in. - 2 ft. 0 in., 12-24 in) is the anchor. RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (about 3.9-19.7 in); Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited) gives "Height: 1.00 to 2.00 feet" (agreeing with NC State) but "Spread: 1.00 to 1.50 feet" (12-18 in); Clemson says the blooms are "on spikes 12 to 18 inches tall". The 24 in spread maximum rests on NC State alone.

No admissible source gave a fertilizing rate or schedule for this species; UGA's bulb bulletin is multi-species and not used. Humidity, day and night growing temperatures and indoor light are not addressed for this outdoor bulb. NC State's only temperature figures are its cold-damage range ("They range from semi-hardy (damaged below 28 degrees F) to hardy (injured below 5 degrees F).", see chill_damage_f) and its Bulb Storage value "Store bulbs dry at 45-55°F"; neither is a growing-temperature range.

NC State's other listed names (Equinox Flower, Hurricane Lily, Naked Lily, Red Magic Lily, Red Surprise Lily, Spider Lily) may overlap names used for other Lycoris species or other genera; Missouri Botanical Garden (read in a browser at audit; not cited) notes "Plants in the genus Lycoris are sometimes commonly called resurrection flower, surprise lily, magic lily or naked ladies because the leaves disappear in summer with the flower spikes seemingly rising from the dead in late summer." None is used as the primary name, and nothing was taken from sibling pages.

RHS's Potentially harmful text, glove warning and Pets line included, appears word for word on RHS's Lycoris aurea page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/71559/lycoris-aurea/details), as does its Cultivation paragraph, so it is RHS's shared Lycoris wording rather than a finding specific to L. radiata; NC State's poison block is the species-specific evidence.
